lessons.title: Components, displacements and unit vectors
lessons.summary: Use 2D and 3D vectors to describe position, displacement, length and midpoint.
lessons.objective: Use 2D and 3D vectors to describe position, displacement, length and midpoint.
lessons.before: Check the order and sign of the components before writing equations.
lessons.ideas:
Unit vectors \(\mathbf i,\mathbf j,\mathbf k\) point along the positive axes. In 2D use two components. In 3D use three, including a zero for any direction with no movement.

\(\overrightarrow{AB}=\overrightarrow{OB}-\overrightarrow{OA}\). The arrow reads start to finish, while the subtraction reads finish minus start.

The parallelogram diagonal is the sum of the adjacent side vectors. A negative scalar reverses direction as it changes length.

For non-zero \(\mathbf d\), the unit vector along it is \(\frac{\mathbf d}{|\mathbf d|}\). For the opposite unit vector, use \(-\frac{\mathbf d}{|\mathbf d|}\).

\(\overrightarrow{OM}=\overrightarrow{OA}+\tfrac12\overrightarrow{AB}=\tfrac12(\overrightarrow{OA}+\overrightarrow{OB})\).
lessons.method:
1. An ordered list of components describes a movement. The point \(P(2,-1,3)\) has position vector \(\overrightarrow{OP}\). The same column can describe a displacement between other points.

  2. Think of a route from the origin. Going to \(A\) and then moving by \(\overrightarrow{AB}\) must arrive at \(B\). Reversing the route negates the displacement.

  3. To take two steps, translate the second arrow so it starts at the first arrow’s tip. To multiply by a scalar, multiply all the components by that number.

  4. Use Pythagoras on mutually perpendicular axes. The length is \(\sqrt{x^2+y^2+z^2}\) in 3D. In 2D omit the last term. A direction without its original speed or length can be given by a unit vector.

  5. Start at \(A\) and take half the displacement to \(B\). This gives an average of the endpoint position vectors, and it works in either dimension.
mistakes: Keep the coordinate order when switching forms. In \(2\mathbf i-3\mathbf k\), the second component is zero.
Subtracting \(\overrightarrow{OB}\) from \(\overrightarrow{OA}\) gives \(\overrightarrow{BA}\). A distance check alone cannot spot this reversal.
Scaling one component alone generally changes the direction, so it does not give a parallel vector.
The zero vector has length zero and no direction. Dividing it by its length does not define a unit vector.
Half of \(\overrightarrow{AB}\) is a displacement from \(A\), not usually a position from \(O\).

examples.title: Read the basis components
examples.question: Write \(3 \mathbf i - 5 \mathbf k\) as a column vector. Give all 3 components.
examples.solution:
The coefficients of \(\mathbf i,\mathbf j,\mathbf k\) give the components in that order.

The column vector is \(\begin{pmatrix}3\\0\\-5\end{pmatrix}\).

examples.title: Find endpoint minus start point
examples.question: Find \(\overrightarrow{AB}\) for \(A(2, -3, 5)\) and \(B(-4, 1, 2)\).
examples.solution:
The movement must start at \(A\) and finish at \(B\). Subtract the starting position from the ending position.

\(\overrightarrow{AB}=\begin{pmatrix}-4\\1\\2\end{pmatrix}-\begin{pmatrix}2\\-3\\5\end{pmatrix}=\begin{pmatrix}-6\\4\\-3\end{pmatrix}\).

examples.title: Find endpoint minus start point
examples.question: Find \(\overrightarrow{AB}\) for \(A(6, -3)\) and \(B(-2, 0)\).
examples.solution:
The movement must start at \(A\) and finish at \(B\). Subtract the starting position from the ending position.

\(\overrightarrow{AB}=\begin{pmatrix}-2\\0\end{pmatrix}-\begin{pmatrix}6\\-3\end{pmatrix}=\begin{pmatrix}-8\\3\end{pmatrix}\).

examples.title: Combine two vectors
examples.question: Given \(\mathbf a=\begin{pmatrix}1\\4\\-2\end{pmatrix},\quad\mathbf b=\begin{pmatrix}-3\\0\\5\end{pmatrix}\), calculate \(2 \mathbf a - 3 \mathbf b\). Give all components.
examples.solution:
Scale every component before adding or subtracting.

\(2 \mathbf a - 3 \mathbf b=2\begin{pmatrix}1\\4\\-2\end{pmatrix}-3\begin{pmatrix}-3\\0\\5\end{pmatrix}=\begin{pmatrix}11\\8\\-19\end{pmatrix}\).

lessons.title: Vector equations of straight lines
lessons.summary: Build line equations from points and directions, test membership and restrict parameters to a segment.
lessons.objective: Build line equations from points and directions, test membership and restrict parameters to a segment.
lessons.before: Check the order and sign of the components before writing equations.
lessons.ideas:
The position vector \(\mathbf r\) changes with \(t\). A whole straight line uses all real values of \(t\), including negative values.

For distinct points \(A\) and \(B\), one form is \(\mathbf r=\overrightarrow{OA}+t\overrightarrow{AB}\). In this form, \(t=0\) gives \(A\) and \(t=1\) gives \(B\).

In a fixed coordinate, the direction component is zero. That coordinate must equal the anchor coordinate at every point of the line.

If \(\mathbf b=\mathbf a+s\mathbf d\), then \(\mathbf b+u(c\mathbf d)\) equals \(\mathbf a+(s+cu)\mathbf d\). With \(c\ne0\), the parameter \(s+cu\) ranges over every real number.

\(0\le t\le1\) describes the closed segment for this particular choice of anchor and direction. At \(t=\tfrac12\), the point is the midpoint.
lessons.method:
1. In \(\mathbf r=\mathbf a+t\mathbf d\), \(\mathbf a\) fixes the position at \(t=0\), and non-zero \(\mathbf d\) gives the direction of movement as \(t\) increases.

  2. Either point can anchor the line. Take the difference of the two position vectors to get a direction. Swapping their order reverses the arrow along the same line.

  3. Write the three coordinate equations and use a changing coordinate to get a candidate parameter. All coordinates must agree at that same value.

  4. Choose another anchor already on the line, and scale the direction by a non-zero number. The new parameter still traces all the same points.

  5. The entire line through \(A\) and \(B\) also extends beyond its endpoints. In the parameterisation from \(A\) along the full displacement \(\overrightarrow{AB}\), the endpoints are \(t=0\) and \(t=1\).
mistakes: A negative parameter moves in the opposite sense from the direction arrow. The direction vector does not have to have length one.
Using a second position vector as the direction only works in special cases. Start with endpoint minus start point.
Separate values of \(t\) for different coordinates never establish membership.
A parallel direction alone does not establish that two equations describe the same line. The anchor must be on the original line.
With a different direction scale, the parameter of \(B\) may no longer be \(1\). Find it before restricting the parameter.

examples.title: Read a point from its parameter
examples.question: A line has equation \(\mathbf r=\begin{pmatrix}3\\1\\-2\end{pmatrix}+t\begin{pmatrix}-4\\2\\1\end{pmatrix}\). Find the point at \(t=-2\). Give all coordinates.
examples.solution:
Substitute the same parameter into all coordinates.

\(\mathbf r=\begin{pmatrix}3\\1\\-2\end{pmatrix}+\left(-2\right)\begin{pmatrix}-4\\2\\1\end{pmatrix}=\begin{pmatrix}11\\-3\\-4\end{pmatrix}\).

The point is \(P(11, -3, -4)\).

examples.title: Write a line through two points
examples.question: Use \(A(2, 1, -4)\) and \(B(6, -5, -2)\) to construct \(\mathbf r=\mathbf a+t\mathbf d\). Take the anchor at \(A\) and use \(\overrightarrow{AB}\) as the direction. Give every component of both vectors.
examples.solution:
Use the position of \(A\) for the anchor.

\(\overrightarrow{AB}=\begin{pmatrix}4\\-6\\2\end{pmatrix}\) by subtracting the starting position from the final one.

The line is \(\mathbf r=\begin{pmatrix}2\\1\\-4\end{pmatrix}+t\begin{pmatrix}4\\-6\\2\end{pmatrix}\).

examples.title: Write a line through two points
examples.question: Use \(A(1, 6)\) and \(B(-5, 8)\) to construct \(\mathbf r=\mathbf a+t\mathbf d\). Take the anchor at \(A\) and use \(\overrightarrow{AB}\) as the direction. Give every component of both vectors.
examples.solution:
Use the position of \(A\) for the anchor.

\(\overrightarrow{AB}=\begin{pmatrix}-6\\2\end{pmatrix}\) by subtracting the starting position from the final one.

The line is \(\mathbf r=\begin{pmatrix}1\\6\end{pmatrix}+t\begin{pmatrix}-6\\2\end{pmatrix}\).

examples.title: Test point membership
examples.question: A line has equation \(\mathbf r=\begin{pmatrix}0\\-4\\7\end{pmatrix}+t\begin{pmatrix}0\\2\\-3\end{pmatrix}\). Find the parameter of \(P(0, -8, 13)\) and verify the other coordinates.
examples.solution:
The y-coordinate requires \(2 t - 4=-8\), so \(t=-2\).

Test the same value in the full equation. It gives \(\begin{pmatrix}0\\-8\\13\end{pmatrix}\), which matches all the coordinates.

The point lies on the line at \(t=-2\).

lessons.title: Scalar products, angles and perpendicularity
lessons.summary: Use scalar products to find directed vector angles, smaller line angles and perpendicular directions.
lessons.objective: Use scalar products to find directed vector angles, smaller line angles and perpendicular directions.
lessons.before: Check the order and sign of the components before writing equations.
lessons.ideas:
With \(\mathbf a=(a_x,a_y,a_z)\) and \(\mathbf b=(b_x,b_y,b_z)\) written as component triples, \(\mathbf a\cdot\mathbf b=a_xb_x+a_yb_y+a_zb_z\).

\(\cos\theta=\frac{\mathbf a\cdot\mathbf b}{|\mathbf a||\mathbf b|}\), with \(0^\circ\le\theta\le180^\circ\). A negative dot product gives an obtuse angle unless the arrows point in exactly opposite directions.

Use \(\cos\theta=\frac{|\mathbf d_1\cdot\mathbf d_2|}{|\mathbf d_1||\mathbf d_2|}\) to get \(0^\circ\le\theta\le90^\circ\).

For directions \(\mathbf a\) and \(\mathbf b\), use \(\mathbf a\cdot\mathbf b=0\). For two lines to meet at a right angle, also establish that they intersect.

The signed component of \(\mathbf a\) along non-zero \(\mathbf d\) is \(\mathbf a\cdot\frac{\mathbf d}{|\mathbf d|}\). It equals \(|\mathbf a|\cos\theta\).
lessons.method:
1. Multiply matching components and add the products. The resulting scalar can be negative, zero or positive.

  2. Put both vector arrows tail to tail. For non-zero vectors, divide the dot product by the two positive magnitudes to get the cosine of their angle.

  3. A direction vector can be reversed without changing a line. The angle between two lines is the smaller angle made by a pair of their directions, whether or not the lines meet.

  4. The dot product of non-zero vectors vanishes exactly when the cosine of their angle is zero. This gives an equation for unknown components.

  5. Taking the dot product with a unit direction gives the signed length of a component. A negative result means the component points against the chosen direction.
mistakes: Elementwise products alone give three values. Add them to finish the dot product.
Do not remove a negative sign from the dot product when the question asks for the angle between directed vectors.
The anchor points do not describe the inclinations of the lines. Use their direction vectors, and round the angle only at the end.
The zero vector has zero dot product with every vector but defines no angle.
A negative signed component is useful information. An actual distance is never negative.

examples.title: Find the scalar product
examples.question: Calculate \(\mathbf a\cdot\mathbf b\) for \(\mathbf a=\begin{pmatrix}3\\-1\\4\end{pmatrix}\) and \(\mathbf b=\begin{pmatrix}-2\\5\\3\end{pmatrix}\).
examples.solution:
Multiply corresponding components, then add.

\(\mathbf a\cdot\mathbf b=\left(3\right)\left(-2\right)+\left(-1\right)\left(5\right)+\left(4\right)\left(3\right)=1\).

examples.title: Find the angle between two vectors
examples.question: Find the angle \(\theta\) between the vectors \(\begin{pmatrix}4\\1\\-2\end{pmatrix}\) and \(\begin{pmatrix}-1\\3\\1\end{pmatrix}\). Give your answer in degrees to one decimal place.
examples.solution:
Keep the sign of the scalar product \(-3\) because the two vector arrows have fixed directions.

The magnitudes are \(\sqrt{21}\) and \(\sqrt{11}\), giving \(\cos\theta=- \frac{\sqrt{231}}{77}\).

Therefore \(\theta=101.4^\circ\).

examples.title: Find the angle between two vectors
examples.question: Find the angle \(\theta\) between the vectors \(\begin{pmatrix}1\\1\\-2\end{pmatrix}\) and \(\begin{pmatrix}2\\-3\\4\end{pmatrix}\). Give your answer in degrees to one decimal place.
examples.solution:
Keep the sign of the scalar product \(-9\) because the two vector arrows have fixed directions.

The magnitudes are \(\sqrt{6}\) and \(\sqrt{29}\), giving \(\cos\theta=- \frac{3 \sqrt{174}}{58}\).

Therefore \(\theta=133.0^\circ\).

examples.title: Find the smaller line angle
examples.question: Find the smaller angle \(\theta\) between \(l_1: \mathbf r=\begin{pmatrix}1\\0\\2\end{pmatrix}+t\begin{pmatrix}1\\-2\\3\end{pmatrix}\) and \(l_2: \mathbf r=\begin{pmatrix}0\\2\\-1\end{pmatrix}+u\begin{pmatrix}-3\\0\\-1\end{pmatrix}\). Give your answer in degrees to one decimal place.
examples.solution:
Use the direction vectors. Their dot product is \(-6\). The absolute value gives the smaller angle because either direction can represent a line.

The magnitudes are \(\sqrt{14}\) and \(\sqrt{10}\), giving \(\cos\theta=\frac{3 \sqrt{35}}{35}\).

Therefore \(\theta=59.5^\circ\).

lessons.title: Parallel, intersecting and skew lines
lessons.summary: Classify two lines in space, verify coordinate consistency and find an intersection when it exists.
lessons.objective: Classify two lines in space, verify coordinate consistency and find an intersection when it exists.
lessons.before: Check the order and sign of the components before writing equations.
lessons.ideas:
If \(\mathbf e=c\mathbf d\), test whether the difference of the anchors also equals a scalar times \(\mathbf d\). If it does, the lines are coincident.

Look for two scalar relationships, one between the directions and one between the anchor displacement and a direction.

Solve two independent coordinate equations, then verify the unused one. Substitute the parameter into either full line equation to state the intersection.

Skew means non-parallel and non-intersecting. Show both facts from the direction and coordinate tests.

For non-parallel directions, some pair of coordinate equations is independent. Use that pair to determine both parameters before the final check.
lessons.method:
1. Check whether the second direction equals a non-zero scalar times the first. Then distinguish a single common line from two distinct parallel lines.

  2. A point of one parallel line lies on the other precisely when the two lines coincide. Check the anchor difference to show this directly.

  3. For non-parallel directions, a shared point can occur only once. Use two separate parameters, one for each line. Equate their three coordinate expressions.

  4. Two non-parallel lines in 3D can miss each other. If the only candidate from two independent equations fails the third, the lines are skew.

  5. If solving the first two coordinate equations gives the same condition twice, use another coordinate equation. If two equations are inconsistent, there can be no intersection.
mistakes: A zero component calls for a direct comparison. Do not divide by it.
Different anchor points do not rule out coincident lines.
Reporting only the two parameter values does not answer a question asking for the point of intersection.
An apparent crossing in a 2D drawing does not prove that the lines share the same third coordinate.
A mismatch in an equation with no parameters also rules out intersection. Do not discard a fixed coordinate.

examples.title: Classify a pair of lines
examples.question: Classify the lines \(l_1: \mathbf r=\begin{pmatrix}1\\-2\\4\end{pmatrix}+t\begin{pmatrix}2\\0\\3\end{pmatrix}\) and \(l_2: \mathbf r=\begin{pmatrix}4\\-1\\3\end{pmatrix}+u\begin{pmatrix}-4\\0\\-6\end{pmatrix}\).
examples.solution:
The second direction is \(-2\) times the first. Test the displacement between anchors \(\begin{pmatrix}3\\1\\-1\end{pmatrix}\) against that direction.

The lines are distinct and parallel. Their anchor displacement is not a multiple of the direction.

examples.title: Classify a pair of lines
examples.question: Classify the lines \(l_1: \mathbf r=\begin{pmatrix}0\\2\\-3\end{pmatrix}+t\begin{pmatrix}2\\-1\\0\end{pmatrix}\) and \(l_2: \mathbf r=\begin{pmatrix}6\\-1\\-3\end{pmatrix}+u\begin{pmatrix}-4\\2\\0\end{pmatrix}\).
examples.solution:
The second direction is \(-2\) times the first. Test the displacement between anchors \(\begin{pmatrix}6\\-3\\0\end{pmatrix}\) against that direction.

The lines are coincident. Both anchors lie on the same line and its directions are parallel.

examples.title: Classify a pair of lines
examples.question: Classify the lines \(l_1: \mathbf r=\begin{pmatrix}2\\-3\\4\end{pmatrix}+t\begin{pmatrix}4\\-2\\1\end{pmatrix}\) and \(l_2: \mathbf r=\begin{pmatrix}-2\\-1\\3\end{pmatrix}+u\begin{pmatrix}-8\\4\\-2\end{pmatrix}\).
examples.solution:
The second direction is \(-2\) times the first. Test the displacement between anchors \(\begin{pmatrix}-4\\2\\-1\end{pmatrix}\) against that direction.

The lines are coincident. Both anchors lie on the same line and its directions are parallel.

examples.title: Classify a pair of lines
examples.question: Classify the lines \(l_1: \mathbf r=\begin{pmatrix}1\\-2\\4\end{pmatrix}+t\begin{pmatrix}2\\3\\-1\end{pmatrix}\) and \(l_2: \mathbf r=\begin{pmatrix}3\\5\\4\end{pmatrix}+u\begin{pmatrix}-2\\1\\2\end{pmatrix}\). Give all coordinates of their intersection.
examples.solution:
Directions are not proportional. Equate coordinates, keeping separate parameters for the two lines.

Solve \(2 t + 1=3 - 2 u\) and \(3 t - 2=u + 5\) to get \(t=2\) and \(u=-1\).

The remaining z-coordinates are \(2\) and \(2\).

All three coordinates match. The lines intersect at \((5, 4, 2)\).

lessons.title: Foot of a perpendicular and point-to-line distance
lessons.summary: Find the foot on a line, prove the nearest distance and use the method on spatial diagonals.
lessons.objective: Find the foot on a line, prove the nearest distance and use the method on spatial diagonals.
lessons.before: Check the order and sign of the components before writing equations.
lessons.ideas:
For \(\mathbf f=\mathbf a+t\mathbf d\) and point \(P\) with position vector \(\mathbf p\), solve \((\mathbf p-\mathbf f)\cdot\mathbf d=0\).

When \(\mathbf d\ne\mathbf 0\), the equation gives exactly one value \(t=\frac{(\mathbf p-\mathbf a)\cdot\mathbf d}{\mathbf d\cdot\mathbf d}\).

After locating \(F\), the point-to-line distance is \(|\mathbf p-\mathbf f|\). If \(P\) already lies on the line, the foot is \(P\) and the distance is zero.

Choose a clear origin and keep the same coordinate order throughout. Use the full spatial direction of the edge or diagonal in the dot product.

If \(\mathbf r=\overrightarrow{OA}+t\overrightarrow{AB}\), a foot with \(0\le t\le1\) lies on segment \(AB\).
lessons.method:
1. Write the foot \(F\) as a general point on the line. The displacement from \(F\) to \(P\) must be perpendicular to the line direction.

  2. A foot must lie on the given line and make a right angle with it. Solve for the parameter first and substitute back into the line. Test both conditions if a point has already been proposed.

  3. For any other point \(X\) on the line, triangle \(PFX\) is right-angled at \(F\). So \(PX^2=PF^2+FX^2\), and any non-zero \(FX\) increases the distance.

  4. Assign axes along mutually perpendicular edges. For a cuboid, the coordinates of each vertex can then be read from its side lengths. Build the line and perpendicular condition from these coordinates.

  5. For application questions on a finite segment, use the closest point on its supporting line first. If the foot lies outside the segment, compare the endpoints or use \(PX^2=PF^2+FX^2\) to choose the closer endpoint.
mistakes: \(\mathbf p-\mathbf a\) is the movement from the anchor to \(P\). The perpendicular condition uses the unknown \(F\), not the anchor.
The denominator is the square of the direction’s length. A non-unit direction cannot be treated as a unit direction.
Distance to a chosen anchor is generally longer than distance to the line. Calculate the foot first.
A diagram flattens depth. A visual right angle is only a cue, while the dot product verifies the calculation.
Do not report a foot outside the segment as a point of that segment.

examples.title: Drop a perpendicular from a point
examples.question: For \(P(5, 2, 6)\) and the line \(\mathbf r=\begin{pmatrix}1\\-1\\2\end{pmatrix}+t\begin{pmatrix}2\\1\\-1\end{pmatrix}\), find the foot of the perpendicular \(F\). Give the parameter and every coordinate of \(F\).
examples.solution:
Put \(\mathbf f=\begin{pmatrix}1\\-1\\2\end{pmatrix}+t\begin{pmatrix}2\\1\\-1\end{pmatrix}\) on the line. The displacement from \(F\) to \(P\) must be perpendicular to its direction.

Set the scalar product to zero. This gives \(7 - 6 t=0\), so \(t=\frac{7}{6}\).

Substitute into the line to obtain \(F(\frac{10}{3}, \frac{1}{6}, \frac{5}{6})\).

The perpendicular foot is \(F(\frac{10}{3}, \frac{1}{6}, \frac{5}{6})\) at \(t=\frac{7}{6}\).

examples.title: Drop a perpendicular from a point
examples.question: For \(P(6, 0, 2)\) and the line \(\mathbf r=\begin{pmatrix}2\\3\\1\end{pmatrix}+t\begin{pmatrix}0\\3\\-2\end{pmatrix}\), find the foot of the perpendicular \(F\). Give the parameter and every coordinate of \(F\).
examples.solution:
Put \(\mathbf f=\begin{pmatrix}2\\3\\1\end{pmatrix}+t\begin{pmatrix}0\\3\\-2\end{pmatrix}\) on the line. The displacement from \(F\) to \(P\) must be perpendicular to its direction.

Set the scalar product to zero. This gives \(- 13 t - 11=0\), so \(t=- \frac{11}{13}\).

Substitute into the line to obtain \(F(2, \frac{6}{13}, \frac{35}{13})\).

The perpendicular foot is \(F(2, \frac{6}{13}, \frac{35}{13})\) at \(t=- \frac{11}{13}\).

examples.title: Drop a perpendicular from a point
examples.question: For \(P(5, -4, 2)\) and the line \(\mathbf r=\begin{pmatrix}2\\3\\0\end{pmatrix}+t\begin{pmatrix}3\\1\\-2\end{pmatrix}\), find the foot of the perpendicular \(F\). Give the parameter and every coordinate of \(F\).
examples.solution:
Put \(\mathbf f=\begin{pmatrix}2\\3\\0\end{pmatrix}+t\begin{pmatrix}3\\1\\-2\end{pmatrix}\) on the line. The displacement from \(F\) to \(P\) must be perpendicular to its direction.

Set the scalar product to zero. This gives \(- 14 t - 2=0\), so \(t=- \frac{1}{7}\).

Substitute into the line to obtain \(F(\frac{11}{7}, \frac{20}{7}, \frac{2}{7})\).

The perpendicular foot is \(F(\frac{11}{7}, \frac{20}{7}, \frac{2}{7})\) at \(t=- \frac{1}{7}\).

examples.title: Drop a perpendicular from a point
examples.question: For \(P(5, 1, 2)\) and the line \(\mathbf r=\begin{pmatrix}1\\-2\\3\end{pmatrix}+t\begin{pmatrix}2\\0\\1\end{pmatrix}\), find the foot of the perpendicular \(F\) and exact distance \(PF\). Give every coordinate of \(F\).
examples.solution:
Put \(\mathbf f=\begin{pmatrix}1\\-2\\3\end{pmatrix}+t\begin{pmatrix}2\\0\\1\end{pmatrix}\) on the line. The displacement from \(F\) to \(P\) must be perpendicular to its direction.

Set the scalar product to zero. This gives \(7 - 5 t=0\), so \(t=\frac{7}{5}\).

Substitute into the line to obtain \(F(\frac{19}{5}, -2, \frac{22}{5})\).

The foot is \(F(\frac{19}{5}, -2, \frac{22}{5})\) and \(PF=\frac{9 \sqrt{5}}{5}\). Use the magnitude of the perpendicular displacement \(\begin{pmatrix}\frac{6}{5}\\3\\- \frac{12}{5}\end{pmatrix}\).

questions.answer_html: The displacement is \(\begin{pmatrix}-2\\-4\\5\end{pmatrix}\) and \(AB=3 \sqrt{5}\), found by squaring and adding the components before taking the square root.

The displacement is \(\begin{pmatrix}-2\\-4\\5\end{pmatrix}\) and \(AB=3 \sqrt{5}\), found by squaring and adding the components before taking the square root.

questions.title: Find the midpoint
questions.prompt_html: Find the midpoint of \(AB\) when \(A(7, 3, 0)\) and \(B(-2, 1, 4)\). Give all coordinates.
questions.answer_html: The midpoint is \(M(\frac{5}{2}, 2, 2)\).

questions.title: The nearest end of a closed rail
questions.prompt_html:
A rail is the closed segment from \(A(0, 0, 0)\) to \(B(2, 1, 2)\). The point \(P(-2, 1, 0)\) lies off the rail.

  2. Find the point on the rail nearest to \(P\) and its exact distance from \(P\). [3]
questions.answer_html:
(a) The foot parameter is \(-\frac13\), so the foot is outside the parameter interval \([0,1]\).

(b) Because \(PX^2=PF^2+FX^2\), the nearest rail point is \(A(0,0,0)\), at distance \(\sqrt5\).
questions.solution_html:
Part (a)

Put \(\mathbf f=\begin{pmatrix}0\\0\\0\end{pmatrix}+t\begin{pmatrix}2\\1\\2\end{pmatrix}\) on the line. The displacement from \(F\) to \(P\) must be perpendicular to its direction.

Set the scalar product to zero. This gives \(- 9 t - 3=0\), so \(t=- \frac{1}{3}\).

Substitute into the line to obtain \(F(- \frac{2}{3}, - \frac{1}{3}, - \frac{2}{3})\).

The perpendicular foot is \(F(- \frac{2}{3}, - \frac{1}{3}, - \frac{2}{3})\) at \(t=- \frac{1}{3}\).

The foot parameter is \(-\frac13\), so the foot is outside the parameter interval \([0,1]\).

Part (b)

Each rail point has parameter \(t\ge0\), so moving from \(A\) along the rail increases its distance from the foot at \(t=-\frac13\).

Because \(PX^2=PF^2+FX^2\), the nearest rail point is \(A(0,0,0)\), at distance \(\sqrt5\).
